item.title: Simulation of a Battery Cell on Quantum Computers: Reactions & Transport
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Hybrid quantum-classical implementation of the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian solves non-linear transport and reaction PDEs, demonstrating the first quantum simulation of a battery cell using the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe).

Grade 0.396 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Albert J. Pool, Michael Schelling, Birger Horstmann

Asks

Can non-linear partial differential equations modeling electrochemical battery transport and reactions be solved efficiently on quantum hardware?

But

Demonstrated for the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) approximation; tailored to divide non-linear PDE computational tasks for noisy quantum systems.

Tools

Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian · hybrid quantum-classical algorithm · Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe)

Abstract

Simulations of electrochemical materials and systems accelerate technological progress, but are still limited by computational power. In particular, quantum computing offers prospects for higher resolutions, due to the exponential amount of data that can be stored in a quantum state. As current quantum computers are still noisy, we consider a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm, that divides the problem into smaller computational tasks. We describe how to implement such an algorithm for non-linear partial differential equations, the Feynman-Kitaev Hamiltonian, in a scalable way for an electrochemical system. We show how it can evaluate general electrochemical models and present a quantum simulation of the Single Particle Model with electrolyte (SPMe) as the first quantum simulation of a battery cell.

item.title: Influence of fast and slow laser phase noise on the fidelity of the Mølmer-Sørensen trapped-ion gate
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Derives analytical filter functions and error formulas for Mølmer-Sørensen gate fidelity under fast laser phase noise (at trap frequencies) and slow noise (order of 1/τ), giving a simplified error estimate ϵslow∼Δωτ.

Grade 0.345 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Nikita Semenin, Ksenia Khabarova, Nikolay Kolachevsky

Figure

Fast noise filter functions as a function of frequency for phase-sensitive and phase-insensitive geometries, showing peaks centered around the carrier detuning μ with width on the order of 1/τ.

Asks

How do fast and slow laser phase noise components quantitatively impact the fidelity of Mølmer-Sørensen gates across common beam geometries?

Before

was numerical simulations without analytical expressions for fast noise (Nakav 2023) and filter functions restricted to optical path fluctuations (Kang 2023)

But

Assumes common laser source, white-noise approximation above cutoff frequencies of 10–100 Hz, equal intensities of bichromatic components, and finite measurement duration T0.

Tools

Hamiltonian perturbation theory · Filter function formalism · Spectral analysis

Abstract

High-fidelity two-qubit entangling gates are essential for the realization of useful quantum algorithms on quantum processors. The Mølmer-Sørensen (MS) gate has become a common choice for trapped-ion quantum computing due to its resilience to ion temperature and its demonstrated record fidelities. However, the spectral impurity of the driving laser field impacts gate performance, with phase noise influencing the qubit dynamics through mechanisms operating on different timescales. In this work, we present a comprehensive theoretical analysis of laser phase noise in the MS gate, identifying two spectral ranges which influence the gate fidelity the most: "fast" noise at frequencies near the motional mode spectrum, and "slow" noise at frequencies on the order of the inverse gate time. We derive the noise Hamiltonians for two common laser beam geometries and obtain analytical expressions for the average gate error in terms of the laser noise power spectral density and gate parameters. For slowly varying noise spectra, we provide simplified error estimates. In addition, we validate our findings against previously published numerical simulations.

item.title: Certifying fermionic Gaussian states (and a little more) with optimal precision dependence
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Certifies any d-mode pure fermionic Gaussian state to infidelity ϵ and failure probability δ with N≤⌈d(d−1)ϵln⁡1δ⌉ copies, single-qubit measurements (only one adaptive per copy), and O(d3) classical runtime per copy.

Grade 0.341 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Ninnat Dangniam, Laphas Premcharoen, Metrasit Sripech, Thiparat Chotibut

Figure

Spectral gap γ(L) of the certification walk versus mode count d on log-log scales across random Gaussian states, random Slater determinants, 1D spin chains, and theoretical lower bounds.

Asks

Can every fermionic Gaussian state be certified with single-qubit measurements, optimal ϵ−1 precision scaling, and efficient classical processing simultaneously?

Before

was O(d3ϵ−2) with non-adaptive single-qubit measurements (Gluza et al. 2018) or O(dϵ−1) with adaptive measurements on all d−1 qubits and product-basis amplitude oracle access (Gupta et al. 2024)

But

Pure states of definite fermionic parity. Exact worst-case bound holds on specific factorized states; random instances show better empirical scaling.

Tools

quantum state verification · d ↔d-2 down-up Markov chain walk · entropy contraction and variance bounding · Pfaffian computational-basis sampling

Abstract

Fermionic Gaussian states are the workhorse reference states for qubit-based quantum simulation of fermionic systems, yet existing certification protocols either proceed via fidelity estimation, leading to suboptimal sample complexity in the target precision ε, only apply to Haar-typical states, or require adaptive measurements on a large fraction of qubits. We give an adaptive protocol that certifies any d-mode pure fermionic Gaussian state using O(d²ε⁻¹) copies, single-qubit measurements with only one qubit measured adaptively per copy, and O(d³) classical processing time per copy. The ε⁻¹ dependence is optimal for the certification problem, even among strategies using entangled measurements. The sample complexity is controlled by the spectral gap of a d↔d-2 down-up walk---a Markov chain studied in the theory of high-dimensional expanders, equivalent to a two-site Glauber dynamics in statistical physics---relating certification efficiency to relaxation time to equilibrium. The worst-case bound is tight for this protocol and is attained by physically relevant states, including ground states of the fully dimerized Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain and BCS pair states. In contrast, numerics up to d=14 suggest that O(d ε⁻¹) copies suffice to certify Haar-typical Gaussian states, a factor of d improvement over the worst-case bound. Finally, because the bound depends only on the target's computational-basis distribution, the protocol extends to efficiently phase-dressed states---states obtained by injecting an efficiently computable diagonal phase to Gaussian states---with the same sample complexity. The class includes a continuous family of four-mode non-Gaussian magic states for matchgate computation.

item.title: Quantum Simulation of Si/SiGe Devices with Experimentally Calibrated Micromagnet Effects
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Full-stack 3D device simulation incorporates Jiles-Atherton micromagnet hysteresis and semi-empirical parasitic charge screening, matching experimental qubit resonance frequencies across a 6-dot Si/SiGe array and reproducing microwave power chevron Rabi dynamics.

Grade 0.335 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Andrii Sokolov, Conor Power, Mathieu Moras, Claude Rohrbacher, Brian Malone, Sergey Amitonov, Agostino Apra, Amir Sammak, Nodar Samkharadze, Elena Blokhina

Figure

Resonant frequency and magnetic field versus external field calibration (left) and comparison of experimental versus simulated resonant frequencies across all six qubits in the array (right).

Asks

How can theoretical CAD models be calibrated to accurately reproduce experimental electrostatic screening, micromagnet hysteresis, and driven spin dynamics in multi-dot Si/SiGe spin-qubit devices?

But

Model requires empirical calibration of electron affinities, discrete parasitic charge domains, and pre-magnetization history. Residual errors remain bounded by lithography, film thickness, and Co purity variations.

Tools

QTCAD electrostatic solver · COMSOL Multiphysics with Jiles-Atherton hysteresis model · Rotating wave approximation time-dependent Schrödinger solver · 6-dot Si/SiGe heterostructure device

Abstract

Silicon-based spin qubits in Si/SiGe heterostructures are a leading platform for scalable quantum computing, yet bridging the gap between theoretical computer-aided design(CAD) models and experimental reality remains a significant challenge. Standard simulations often fail to capture critical physical phenomena, such as interface dipoles, parasitic charge accumulation, and the magnetic hysteresis of on-chip micromagnets. In this work, we present a comprehensive, experimentally calibrated 3D simulation pipeline for a 6-dot Si/SiGe device. We refine the semiconductor band alignment and introduce a semi-empirical classical charge screening model to accurately capture the formation of parasitic wells and their suppression of gate lever-arms. Furthermore, we apply the Jiles-Atherton model to account for the hysteresis and pre-magnetization of integrated cobalt micromagnets, successfully reproducing the experimental resonant frequencies across all six qubits. By coupling these calibrated electrostatic and magnetic profiles into a time-dependent rotating wave approximation (RWA) Hamiltonian, we reproduce experimental observables, including microwave power chevrons. This framework provides a robust foundation for predicting device behavior, evaluating microwave line losses, and optimizing future scalable spin qubit architectures prior to fabrication.
